newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen buying aluminium as summer looms.
newsitem.headline: China seen buying aluminium as summer looms.

text.p: China is buying aluminium on the world market, gearing up for high summer demand, traders in the Far East said on Monday.
Monthly imports of aluminium ingot, much of it from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), would average 40,000 tonnes throughout 1997, a Chinese trading source said.
Latest figures from Chinese customs showed imports of unwrought aluminium and aluminium materials reached 37,847 tonnes in January 1997, up 28.7 percent compared with January 1996.
Imports of unwrought aluminium including alloys rose by 8.8 percent to 15,503 tonnes in January compared with the same period in 1996.
The Chinese source said his company, fully Chinese-owned and based in Hong Kong, handled up to 10 percent of China's annual aluminium imports.
"We're expecting Chinese demand to be 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes for the year," he said.
Aluminium ingot sales to China by his company in February totalled around 4,000 tonnes, he told Reuters by telephone.
Inquiries came from Chinese smelters and trading houses, he said, adding that many Chinese buyers preferred the cheaper CIS product to higher quality Western metal.
"The premium on good Western is around $100 a tonne (to Chinese ports), and on the CIS product around $70-80, so demand for the cheaper product is good," he said.
"The Chinese have basically pushed the aluminium price up," Vinod Kumar, managing director of Donald Mcarthy in Singapore, told Reuters.
"Aluminium premiums have also gone up in Taiwan, Korea and many other places," he said. "The material we were selling to Taiwan at a premium of $65-70 a tonne, we are now selling at $90-95."
Premiums to Korea were $100 above the London Metal Exchange (LME) cash settlement price, he said, and to Hong Kong $90, basis c&f (cost and freight).
The approach of summer would see Chinese demand for aluminium pick up, with consumption concentrated in beverage cans, air-conditioners and refrigerators, traders said.
The approach of warmer weather also saw construction picking up, they said, which would further stimulate demand.
Three months aluminium on the LME was up $8 a tonne at 0855 GMT on Monday from Friday's late close, at $1,666/68.
A dealer there said good consumer buying was seen both in the primary and alloy markets, though good forward selling was still capping the upside.
